docs.title: Welcome to headscale
docs.text:
Headscale is an open source, self-hosted implementation of the Tailscale control server.

This page contains the documentation for the latest version of headscale. Please also check our FAQ.

Join our Discord server for a chat and community support.

docs.title: Design goal
docs.text: Headscale aims to implement a self-hosted, open source alternative to the Tailscale control server. Headscale's goal is to provide self-hosters and hobbyists with an open-source server they can use for their projects and labs. It implements a narrow scope, a single Tailscale network (tailnet), suitable for a personal use, or a small open-source organisation.

docs.title: Update clients
docs.text:
Tailscale clients can update themselves. auto_update.enabled: true in the configuration file turns auto-updates on by default, but a node takes the default only while its own setting is unset. Once it has stored a value, from an earlier default or from tailscale set --auto-update, it keeps it. Headscale always sends a default, so turning the option on later does not reach nodes that joined while it was off.

A connected node can also be asked to update right away:

headscale nodes update-client --identifier <NODE_ID>

The node must allow remote updates (tailscale set --auto-update) and run on a platform that can update itself. As on Tailscale, a node that does not, is not connected, or refuses (for example, with active Tailscale SSH sessions) is answered "not found". Headscale logs the reason a node gives. The command returns once the update has started.

The same request is available in the API as POST /api/v2/device/<NODE_ID>/update-client, with no body. It needs an API key or an OAuth token with the devices:core scope. GET /api/v2/device/<NODE_ID>/update-status answers {"status": "updating"} from a started update until the node runs another version, for at most 10 minutes, and {"status": "not-updating"} otherwise. It needs the devices:core:read scope.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Headscale is "Open Source, acknowledged contribution", this means that any contribution will have to be discussed with the maintainers before being added to the project. This model has been chosen to reduce the risk of burnout by limiting the maintenance overhead of reviewing and validating third-party code.

docs.title: Why do we have this model?
docs.text:
Headscale has a small maintainer team that tries to balance working on the project, fixing bugs and reviewing contributions.

When we work on issues ourselves, we develop first hand knowledge of the code and it makes it possible for us to maintain and own the code as the project develops.

Code contributions are seen as a positive thing. People enjoy and engage with our project, but it also comes with some challenges; we have to understand the code, we have to understand the feature, we might have to become familiar with external libraries or services and we think about security implications. All those steps are required during the reviewing process. After the code has been merged, the feature has to be maintained. Any changes reliant on external services must be updated and expanded accordingly.

The review and day-1 maintenance adds a significant burden on the maintainers. Often we hope that the contributor will help out, but we found that most of the time, they disappear after their new feature was added.

This means that when someone contributes, we are mostly happy about it, but we do have to run it through a series of checks to establish if we actually can maintain this feature.

docs.title: What do we require?
docs.text:
A general description is provided here and an explicit list is provided in our pull request template.

All new features have to start out with a design document, which should be discussed on the issue tracker (not discord). It should include a use case for the feature, how it can be implemented, who will implement it and a plan for maintaining it.

All features have to be end-to-end tested (integration tests) and have good unit test coverage to ensure that they work as expected. This will also ensure that the feature continues to work as expected over time. If a change cannot be tested, a strong case for why this is not possible needs to be presented.

The contributor should help to maintain the feature over time. In case the feature is not maintained probably, the maintainers reserve themselves the right to remove features they redeem as unmaintainable. This should help to improve the quality of the software and keep it in a maintainable state.

docs.title: Why is 'acknowledged contribution' the chosen model?
docs.text:
Both maintainers have full-time jobs and families, and we want to avoid burnout. We also want to avoid frustration from contributors when their PRs are not accepted.

We are more than happy to exchange emails, or to have dedicated calls before a PR is submitted.

docs.title: When/Why is Feature X going to be implemented?
docs.text:
We use GitHub Milestones to plan for upcoming Headscale releases. Have a look at our current plan to get an idea when a specific feature is about to be implemented. The release plan is subject to change at any time.

If you're interested in contributing, please post a feature request about it. Please be aware that there are a number of reasons why we might not accept specific contributions:

  • It is not possible to implement the feature in a way that makes sense in a self-hosted environment.
  • Given that we are reverse-engineering Tailscale to satisfy our own curiosity, we might be interested in implementing the feature ourselves.
  • You are not sending unit and integration tests with it.

docs.title: Do you support Y method of deploying headscale?
docs.text:
We currently support deploying headscale using our binaries and the DEB packages. Visit our installation guide using official releases for more information.

In addition to that, you may use packages provided by the community or from distributions. Learn more in the installation guide using community packages.

For convenience, we also build container images with headscale. But please be aware that we don't officially support deploying headscale using Docker. On our Discord server we have a "docker-issues" channel where you can ask for Docker-specific help to the community.

docs.title: What is the recommended update path? Can I skip multiple versions while updating?
docs.text:
Please follow the steps outlined in the upgrade guide to update your existing Headscale installation. Its required to update from one stable version to the next (e.g. 0.26.0 → 0.27.1 → 0.28.0) without skipping minor versions in between. You should always pick the latest available patch release.

Be sure to check the changelog for version specific upgrade instructions and breaking changes.

docs.title: Scaling / How many clients does Headscale support?
docs.text:
It depends. As often stated, Headscale is not enterprise software and our focus is homelabbers and self-hosters. Of course, we do not prevent people from using it in a commercial/professional setting and often get questions about scaling.

Please note that when Headscale is developed, performance is not part of the consideration as the main audience is considered to be users with a modest amount of devices. We focus on correctness and feature parity with Tailscale SaaS over time.

To understand if you might be able to use Headscale for your use case, I will describe two scenarios in an effort to explain what is the central bottleneck of Headscale:

  1. An environment with 1000 servers

    • they rarely "move" (change their endpoints)
    • new nodes are added rarely

  2. An environment with 80 laptops/phones (end user devices)

    • nodes move often, e.g. switching from home to office

Headscale calculates a map of all nodes that need to talk to each other, creating this "world map" requires a lot of CPU time. When an event that requires changes to this map happens, the whole "world" is recalculated, and a new "world map" is created for every node in the network.

This means that under certain conditions, Headscale can likely handle 100s of devices (maybe more), if there is little to no change happening in the network. For example, in Scenario 1, the process of computing the world map is extremely demanding due to the size of the network, but when the map has been created and the nodes are not changing, the Headscale instance will likely return to a very low resource usage until the next time there is an event requiring the new map.

In the case of Scenario 2, the process of computing the world map is less demanding due to the smaller size of the network, however, the type of nodes will likely change frequently, which would lead to a constant resource usage.

Headscale will start to struggle when the two scenarios overlap, e.g. many nodes with frequent changes will cause the resource usage to remain constantly high. In the worst case scenario, the queue of nodes waiting for their map will grow to a point where Headscale never will be able to catch up, and nodes will never learn about the current state of the world.

We expect that the performance will improve over time as we improve the code base, but it is not a focus. In general, we will never make the tradeoff to make things faster on the cost of less maintainable or readable code. We are a small team and have to optimise for maintainability.

docs.title: Which database should I use?
docs.text:
We recommend the use of SQLite as database for headscale:

  • SQLite is simple to setup and easy to use
  • It scales well for all of headscale's use cases
  • Development and testing happens primarily on SQLite
  • PostgreSQL is still supported, but is considered to be in "maintenance mode"

The headscale project itself does not provide a tool to migrate from PostgreSQL to SQLite. Please have a look at the related tools documentation for migration tooling provided by the community.

The choice of database has little to no impact on the performance of the server, see Scaling / How many clients does Headscale support? for understanding how Headscale spends its resources.

docs.title: Why is my reverse proxy not working with headscale?
docs.text: We don't know. We don't use reverse proxies with headscale ourselves, so we don't have any experience with them. We have community documentation on how to configure various reverse proxies, and a dedicated "reverse-proxy-issues" channel on our Discord server where you can ask for help to the community.

docs.title: Can I use headscale and tailscale on the same machine?
docs.text: Running headscale on a machine that is also in the tailnet can cause problems with subnet routers, traffic relay nodes, and MagicDNS. It might work, but it is not supported.

docs.title: Why do two nodes see each other in their status, even if a policy rule allows traffic only in one direction?
docs.text:
A frequent use case is to allow traffic only from one node to another, but not the other way around. For example, the workstation of an administrator should be able to connect to all nodes but the nodes themselves shouldn't be able to connect back to the administrator's node. Why do all nodes see the administrator's workstation in the output of tailscale status?

This is essentially how Tailscale works. If traffic is allowed to flow in one direction, then both nodes see each other in their output of tailscale status. Traffic is still filtered according to the policy, with the exception of tailscale ping which is always allowed in either direction.

See also https://tailscale.com/docs/concepts/device-visibility.

docs.title: My policy is stored in the database and Headscale refuses to start due to an invalid policy. How can I recover?
docs.text:
Headscale checks if the policy is valid during startup and refuses to start if it detects an error. The error message indicates which part of the policy is invalid. Follow these steps to fix your policy:

  • Dump the policy to a file: headscale policy get --bypass-server-and-access-database-directly > policy.json
  • Edit and fixup policy.json. Use the command headscale policy check --file policy.json to validate the policy.
  • Load the modified policy: headscale policy set --bypass-server-and-access-database-directly --file policy.json
  • Start Headscale as usual.

Full server configuration required

The above commands to get/set the policy require a complete server configuration file including database settings. A minimal config to control Headscale via remote CLI is not sufficient. You may use headscale -c /path/to/config.yaml to specify the path to an alternative configuration file.

docs.title: How can I migrate back to the recommended IP prefixes?
docs.text:
Tailscale only supports the IP prefixes 100.64.0.0/10 and fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48 or smaller subnets thereof. The following steps can be used to migrate from unsupported IP prefixes back to the supported and recommended ones.

Backup and test in a demo environment required

The commands below update the IP addresses of all nodes in your tailnet and this might have a severe impact in your specific environment. At a minimum:

  • Create a backup of your database
  • Test the commands below in a representive demo environment. This allows to catch subsequent connectivity errors early and see how the tailnet behaves in your specific environment.
  • Stop Headscale
  • Restore the default prefixes in the configuration file: 
    prefixes:
  v4: 100.64.0.0/10
  v6: fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48
  • Update the nodes.ipv4 and nodes.ipv6 columns in the database and assign each node a unique IPv4 and IPv6 address. The following SQL statement assigns IP addresses based on the node ID: 
    UPDATE nodes
SET ipv4=concat('100.64.', id/256, '.', id%256),
    ipv6=concat('fd7a:115c:a1e0::', format('%x', id));
  • Update the policy to reflect the IP address changes (if any)
  • Start Headscale

Nodes should reconnect within a few seconds and pickup their newly assigned IP addresses.

docs.title: How can I avoid to send logs to Tailscale Inc?
docs.text:
A Tailscale client collects logs about its operation and connection attempts with other clients and sends them to a central log service operated by Tailscale Inc.

Headscale, by default, instructs clients to disable log submission to the central log service. This configuration is applied by a client once it successfully connected with Headscale. See the configuration option logtail.enabled in the configuration file for details.

Do not grant the https://tailscale.com/cap/data-plane-audit-logs node attribute while logtail.enabled is false. A client with log submission disabled treats this attribute as "the tailnet requires logging" and turns itself off, as tailscale down would. It stays off until the attribute is removed and tailscale up is run. A client started with TS_NO_LOGS_NO_SUPPORT=true or --no-logs-no-support reacts the same way, whatever logtail.enabled says.

Alternatively, logging can also be disabled on the client side. This is independent of Headscale and opting out of client logging disables log submission early during client startup. The configuration is operating system specific and is usually achieved by:

  • setting the environment variable TS_NO_LOGS_NO_SUPPORT=true or
  • by passing the flag --no-logs-no-support to tailscaled or
  • by disabling "Remote client logging" in the mobile app settings

See https://tailscale.com/docs/features/logging#opt-out-of-client-logging for details.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Headscale aims to implement a self-hosted, open source alternative to the Tailscale control server. Headscale's goal is to provide self-hosters and hobbyists with an open-source server they can use for their projects and labs. This page provides on overview of Headscale's feature and compatibility with the Tailscale control server:

  • Full "base" support of Tailscale's features
  • Node registration
    • Web authentication
    • Pre authenticated key
  • DNS
    • MagicDNS
    • Global and restricted nameservers (split DNS)
    • search domains
    • Extra DNS records (Headscale only)
  • File sharing
    • Taildrive
    • Taildrop
  • Tags
  • Routes
    • Subnet routers
    • Exit nodes
    • Route filtering with Via
  • Dual stack (IPv4 and IPv6)
  • Ephemeral nodes
  • Client updates
  • Embedded DERP server
  • Peer relays
  • Policy (GitHub label "policy")
    • ACLs
    • Grants
    • Some Autogroups
    • Auto approvers for subnet routers and exit nodes
    • Tailscale SSH
    • Node attributes
    • Tests and sshTests
  • Node registration using Single-Sign-On (OpenID Connect) (GitHub label "OIDC")
    • Basic registration
    • Update user profile from identity provider
    • OIDC groups cannot be used in ACLs
  • Funnel (#1040)
  • Serve
  • Network flow logs (#1687)

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Headscale provides a HTTP REST API which may be used to integrate a web interface, remote control Headscale or provide a base for custom integration and tooling.

The API requires a valid API key before use. To create an API key, log into your Headscale server and generate one with the default expiration of 90 days:

headscale apikeys create

Copy the output of the command and save it for later. Please note that you can not retrieve an API key again. If the API key is lost, expire the old one, and create a new one.

To list the API keys currently associated with the server:

headscale apikeys list

and to expire an API key:

headscale apikeys expire --prefix <PREFIX>

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
• API endpoint: /api/v1, e.g. https://headscale.example.com/api/v1
  • Documentation: /api/v1/docs, e.g. https://headscale.example.com/api/v1/docs
  • Headscale Version: /version, e.g. https://headscale.example.com/version
  • Authenticate using HTTP Bearer authentication by sending the API key with the HTTP Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY> header.

Start by creating an API key and test it with the examples below. Read the API documentation provided by your Headscale server at /api/v1/docs for details.

Get details for all usersGet details for user 'bob'Register a node 
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>" \
    https://headscale.example.com/api/v1/user

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>" \
    https://headscale.example.com/api/v1/user?name=bob

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>" \
    --json '{"user": "<USER>", "authId": "<AUTH_ID>"}' \
    https://headscale.example.com/api/v1/auth/register

docs.title: Join nodes with an OAuth client
docs.text:
Headscale also serves a subset of the Tailscale-compatible API at /api/v2, which accepts OAuth 2.0 client-credentials in addition to API keys. The Tailscale client can use an OAuth client secret in place of an auth key: it exchanges the secret for an access token, mints a single-use tagged auth key and registers with it. This works anywhere the client takes an auth key: tailscale up, the container image, tsnet and the tailscale/github-action. One long-lived secret joins any number of nodes. A client keeps its newest 1000 access tokens and minting more ends the oldest, so give a long-lived integration its own client.

Create an OAuth client with the auth_keys scope and the tags its nodes get. The secret is shown once:

headscale oauth-clients create --scope auth_keys --tag tag:ci

Scopes apply to the whole tailnet, as in Tailscale: an auth_keys token can read and revoke auth keys of any tag, an oauth_keys token every OAuth client, and a devices:core:read token reads every device, routes included with fields=all. Keep the secret as safe as any credential that can revoke keys. Without all=true, a token lists only the auth keys made through a token, whatever their tags; with it, every valid auth key. No listing holds a spent, expired or revoked key. Tags limit only the tags a token puts on keys, clients and devices, and which tagged devices it may retag. Deleting an OAuth client revokes its secret and its access tokens; auth keys, clients and nodes created with it stay until you remove them.

Build the auth key from the secret:

  1. Swap the prefix: hskey-client-… becomes tskey-client-…. The client only runs the exchange for tskey-client-; Headscale accepts both.
  2. Append ?baseURL=<your Headscale URL>.
  3. Set --advertise-tags. Each tag must exist in the policy's tagOwners and be one of the OAuth client's tags, or owned by one of them.
tskey-client-<id>-<secret>?baseURL=https://headscale.example.com

Warning

Without baseURL the client sends the secret to https://api.tailscale.com.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
These are all the attributes the client understands; any other is an error. Order does not matter and an empty value means the default.

Attribute Default Effect baseURL https://api.tailscale.com Where the exchange and key creation go. Your Headscale URL, no trailing slash. ephemeral true Node is removed after it goes offline (node.ephemeral.inactivity_timeout). false to keep it. preauthorized false Accepted, no effect: Headscale always authorizes pre-auth-key nodes.

Booleans take any Go strconv.ParseBool value (true, false, 1, 0, …).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
tailscale up, either as the auth key or via --client-secret (which also takes file:/path/to/secret):

tailscale up --login-server https://headscale.example.com --advertise-tags tag:ci \
  --auth-key 'tskey-client-<id>-<secret>?baseURL=https://headscale.example.com&ephemeral=false'

Container image:

docker run -d --name tailscale \
  -e TS_AUTHKEY='tskey-client-<id>-<secret>?baseURL=https://headscale.example.com' \
  -e TS_EXTRA_ARGS='--login-server=https://headscale.example.com --advertise-tags=tag:ci' \
  tailscale/tailscale

tsnet (TS_CLIENT_SECRET works too); import tailscale.com/feature/oauthkey:

srv := &tsnet.Server{
    ControlURL:    "https://headscale.example.com",
    AuthKey:       "tskey-client-<id>-<secret>?baseURL=https://headscale.example.com",
    AdvertiseTags: []string{"tag:ci"},
}

GitHub Action, with the whole string stored as a repository secret:

- uses: tailscale/github-action@v4
  with:
    authkey: ${{ secrets.HEADSCALE_AUTHKEY }}
    args: --login-server=https://headscale.example.com --advertise-tags=tag:ci

Use authkey even though upstream marks it deprecated: oauth-secret appends its own ?… to the secret, which corrupts baseURL.

docs.title: Remote control
docs.text: The headscale binary can control a Headscale instance from a remote machine over the HTTP API.

docs.title: Prerequisite
docs.text:
• A workstation to run headscale (any supported platform, e.g. Linux).
  • The Headscale server reachable over HTTP(S).
  • An API key to authenticate with the Headscale server.

docs.title: Setup remote control
docs.text:
1. Download the headscale binary from GitHub's release page. Make sure to use the same version as on the server.

  2. Put the binary somewhere in your PATH, e.g. /usr/local/bin/headscale

  3. Make headscale executable: chmod +x /usr/local/bin/headscale

  4. Create an API key on the Headscale server.

  5. Provide the connection parameters for the remote Headscale server either via a minimal YAML configuration file or via environment variables:

    Minimal YAML configuration fileEnvironment variables config.yaml
    cli:
    address: <HEADSCALE_URL>
    api_key: <API_KEY>

    export HEADSCALE_CLI_ADDRESS="<HEADSCALE_URL>"
export HEADSCALE_CLI_API_KEY="<API_KEY>"

    This instructs the headscale binary to connect to a remote instance at <HEADSCALE_URL> (e.g. https://headscale.example.com), instead of connecting to the local instance. A bare host without a scheme is assumed to be https.

  6. Test the connection by listing all nodes:

    headscale nodes list

    You should now be able to see a list of your nodes from your workstation, and you can now control the Headscale server from your workstation.

docs.title: Behind a proxy
docs.text: The remote CLI uses the same HTTP API as everything else, so it works through the reverse proxy already in front of Headscale with no extra setup.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Make sure you have the same Headscale version on your server and workstation.
  • Verify that your TLS certificate is valid and trusted.
  • If you don't have access to a trusted certificate (e.g. from Let's Encrypt), either:
    • Add your self-signed certificate to the trust store of your OS or
    • Disable certificate verification by either setting cli.insecure: true in the configuration file or by setting HEADSCALE_CLI_INSECURE=1 via an environment variable. We do not recommend to disable certificate validation.

docs.title: Configuration options
docs.text:
Generated page

This page is generated from the doc comments in hscontrol/types/config.go by go generate ./hscontrol/types/. Edit the comments there, not this page.

Every key headscale reads, in the order headscale generate config prints them, with its type, default, environment variable and an example for a configuration file, the environment and NixOS. Keys that no longer work are listed under Removed keys. Configuration explains where headscale finds its configuration, how to check it, and shows the full example.

docs.title: Value types
docs.text: Type Format Example string Text. Quote it where YAML would read another type, as in "0x1F" or "null". /var/lib/headscale/db.sqlite boolean true or false. true integer A whole number. 1024 duration A number with a unit, ms, s, m, h, d, w or y, units combined largest first; 0 needs none. 1h30m file mode Octal permission bits, quoted. "0770" listen address host:port. An empty host listens on every address; the port may be http or https. 0.0.0.0:8080 URL An absolute http:// or https:// URL with a host. https://headscale.example.com prefix An IP range in CIDR notation. 100.64.0.0/10 secret Text, or file:<path> to read it from a file. file:/run/secrets/oidc_client_secret enum One of the values listed with the key. sqlite DNS record An object with name, type and value. {name: grafana.example.com, type: A, value: 100.64.0.3} value Whatever the setting takes: text, a number, a boolean, a list or a map. file:/run/secrets/cloudflare list A list. A variable holds it as a JSON array or, unless its values are objects, separated by spaces. An empty item is an error. [9.9.9.9, 2620:fe::fe] map Keys you choose, each with a value. A variable holds a JSON object. {corp.example.com: [192.0.2.53]}

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Every key can also be set with an environment variable: HEADSCALE_ and the key's path in capitals, with _ for ., e.g. HEADSCALE_LOG_LEVEL for log.level. Each key below names its variable. A variable wins over the configuration file, which wins over the default. An empty variable, like a key written with no value in the file, counts as unset and keeps the default. A variable set to "" means what "" means in the configuration file: it clears a key with a default, as prefixes.v6: "" does, and is an error where the file's "" is one. A list also clears with []. Quote the value so the quotes reach headscale:

export HEADSCALE_PREFIXES_V6='""'
export HEADSCALE_DERP_URLS='[]'
docker-compose.yaml
environment:
  HEADSCALE_PREFIXES_V6: '""'
  HEADSCALE_DERP_URLS: '[]'

An env file (a Compose env_file, a systemd EnvironmentFile=) and a systemd Environment= strip one level of quotes, so KEY="" there arrives empty and keeps the default: write KEY='""' in an env file and Environment='KEY=""' in a unit.

A list is a JSON array or, unless its values are objects, its values separated by spaces. A map is a JSON object, which replaces the map in the configuration file instead of merging into it. The examples below write every list and map as JSON.

A HEADSCALE_ variable that names no key logs a warning, and one for a removed key also says what to do instead. Other software uses the same prefix, so neither stops headscale.

A DNS provider setting that takes text can also be set on its own as HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_PROVIDER_<SETTING>, e.g. HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_PROVIDER_API_TOKEN; see dns.challenge.provider.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
A secret takes the value itself or file:<path>, which reads it from that file. Environment variables in the path are expanded, as in file:${CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY}/oidc_client_secret, and whitespace around the file's contents is trimmed; an empty file is an error. Headscale reads the file only where the secret is used, and headscale check config and headscale check all never read it. headscale generate config --running and /debug/config show a literal secret as <redacted> and a file: reference as written.

The secrets are database.postgres.pass, oidc.client_secret, cli.api_key and every setting of dns.challenge.provider, where a non-string one, such as acme-dns config, is the JSON in the file.

On NixOS, keep a secret out of the Nix store: load it as a systemd credential and point the key at it.

services.headscale.settings.oidc.client_secret = "file:\${CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY}/oidc_client_secret";
systemd.services.headscale.serviceConfig.LoadCredential = [ "oidc_client_secret:/run/secrets/oidc_client_secret" ];

docs.title: server_url
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Required
  • Env: HEADSCALE_SERVER_URL

The URL clients connect to, with its http:// or https:// scheme, e.g. https://headscale.example.com:443. A trailing slash is trimmed on load. Its host must not be dns.base_domain or a name below it.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS

docs.title: listen_addr
docs.text:
• Type: listen address
  • Default: 0.0.0.0:8080
  • Env: HEADSCALE_LISTEN_ADDR

The host:port the server listens on for clients, the API and the web pages. It serves HTTPS when tls.cert_path or tls.acme.hostname is set, plain HTTP otherwise. The default listens on every address, IPv4 and IPv6 alike.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
listen_addr: 127.0.0.1:8080

export HEADSCALE_LISTEN_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8080

services.headscale.settings.listen_addr = "127.0.0.1:8080";

docs.title: metrics_listen_addr
docs.text:
• Type: listen address
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_METRICS_LISTEN_ADDR

The host:port serving /metrics and /debug; keep it private. Empty disables this listener.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS

export HEADSCALE_METRICS_LISTEN_ADDR=127.0.0.1:9090

services.headscale.settings.metrics_listen_addr = "127.0.0.1:9090";

docs.title: unix_socket
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: /var/run/headscale/headscale.sock
  • Env: HEADSCALE_UNIX_SOCKET

Where the server serves the API without authentication, for the CLI on the same host. The CLI connects to it when cli.address is empty.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
unix_socket: /run/headscale/headscale.sock

export HEADSCALE_UNIX_SOCKET=/run/headscale/headscale.sock

services.headscale.settings.unix_socket = "/run/headscale/headscale.sock";

docs.title: unix_socket_permission
docs.text:
• Type: file mode
  • Default: "0770"
  • Env: HEADSCALE_UNIX_SOCKET_PERMISSION

The file mode of unix_socket, in quoted octal ("0770"): unquoted, YAML reads 0770 as the number 504.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS

docs.title: trusted_proxies
docs.text:
• Type: list of prefixes
  • Default: []
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TRUSTED_PROXIES (space-separated or JSON array)

The CIDRs of reverse proxies whose True-Client-IP, X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For headers are honoured. Empty ignores those headers. Set without a proxy in front, clients can spoof their source IP in logs and the v2 API.

  - 2001:db8::10/128

services.headscale.settings.trusted_proxies = [
  "192.0.2.10/32"
  "2001:db8::10/128"
];

docs.title: node
docs.text:
Covers node key expiry, ephemeral nodes and subnet routes.

All node keys and defaults 
node:
  expiry: 0s
  ephemeral:
    inactivity_timeout: 30m
  routes:
    ha:
      probe_interval: 10s
      probe_timeout: 5s

docs.title: node.expiry
docs.text:
• Type: duration
  • Default: 0s
  • Env: HEADSCALE_NODE_EXPIRY

The key expiry given to a non-tagged node that registers without one, whatever the method (auth key, CLI, web, OIDC). An expiry the client asks for, oidc.use_expiry_from_token and an admin's headscale nodes expire still apply. Tagged nodes never get this default. Zero or negative disables the default.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
node:
  expiry: 2160h

export HEADSCALE_NODE_EXPIRY=2160h

services.headscale.settings.node.expiry = "2160h";

Replaces oidc.expiry (removed).

docs.title: node.ephemeral
docs.text:
Covers ephemeral nodes, which register with an ephemeral auth key and are deleted once they have been offline for node.ephemeral.inactivity_timeout.

All node.ephemeral keys and defaults 
node:
  ephemeral:
    inactivity_timeout: 30m

docs.title: node.ephemeral.inactivity_timeout
docs.text:
• Type: duration
  • Default: 30m
  • Env: HEADSCALE_NODE_EPHEMERAL_INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT

How long an ephemeral node can be offline before it is automatically deleted. It must exceed 65s, the client keepalive plus a margin.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
node:
  ephemeral:
    inactivity_timeout: 1h

export HEADSCALE_NODE_EPHEMERAL_INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT=1h

services.headscale.settings.node.ephemeral.inactivity_timeout = "1h";

Replaces ephemeral_node_inactivity_timeout (removed).

docs.title: node.routes
docs.text:
Covers the routes nodes advertise. See Routes.

All node.routes keys and defaults 
node:
  routes:
    ha:
      probe_interval: 10s
      probe_timeout: 5s

docs.title: node.routes.ha
docs.text:
Health probing of HA subnet routers. When two or more nodes advertise the same route, headscale pings each over Noise and moves the route away from one that does not answer in time. See High availability.

All node.routes.ha keys and defaults 
node:
  routes:
    ha:
      probe_interval: 10s
      probe_timeout: 5s

docs.title: node.routes.ha.probe_interval
docs.text:
• Type: duration
  • Default: 10s
  • Env: HEADSCALE_NODE_ROUTES_HA_PROBE_INTERVAL

How often HA subnet routers are probed; a positive interval must be at least 2s. Zero or negative disables probing, and with it the node.routes.ha.probe_timeout rules.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
node:
  routes:
    ha:
      probe_interval: 30s

export HEADSCALE_NODE_ROUTES_HA_PROBE_INTERVAL=30s

services.headscale.settings.node.routes.ha.probe_interval = "30s";

docs.title: node.routes.ha.probe_timeout
docs.text:
• Type: duration
  • Default: 5s
  • Env: HEADSCALE_NODE_ROUTES_HA_PROBE_TIMEOUT

The maximum time to wait for a probe response before declaring a node unhealthy; at least 1s and less than node.routes.ha.probe_interval.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
node:
  routes:
    ha:
      probe_timeout: 3s

export HEADSCALE_NODE_ROUTES_HA_PROBE_TIMEOUT=3s

services.headscale.settings.node.routes.ha.probe_timeout = "3s";

docs.title: derp
docs.text:
The DERP map: the relay servers clients use when they cannot connect directly, from derp.urls, derp.paths and the embedded server in derp.server. A region replaces an earlier one with the same ID. See DERP.

All derp keys and defaults 
derp:
  server:
    enabled: false
    region_id: 0
    region_code: ""
    region_name: ""
    verify_clients: true
    stun_listen_addr: ""
    private_key_path: ""
    ipv4: ""
    ipv6: ""
    automatically_add_embedded_derp_region: true
  urls:
    - https://controlplane.tailscale.com/derpmap/default
  paths: []
  auto_update_enabled: true
  update_frequency: 3h

docs.title: derp.server
docs.text:
The embedded DERP server, a relay and STUN server run by headscale itself. See Enable embedded DERP.

All derp.server keys and defaults 
derp:
  server:
    enabled: false
    region_id: 0
    region_code: ""
    region_name: ""
    verify_clients: true
    stun_listen_addr: ""
    private_key_path: ""
    ipv4: ""

docs.title: derp.server.enabled
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: false
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_ENABLED

Runs the embedded DERP server. DERP needs TLS, so server_url must be https://.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS

docs.text:
• Type: integer
  • Default: 0
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_REGION_ID

The embedded server's region ID; required and positive when derp.server.enabled is true. Tailscale keeps 900-999 for your own regions. It replaces a region with the same ID from the other sources.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
derp:
  server:
    region_id: 999

export HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_REGION_ID=999

services.headscale.settings.derp.server.region_id = 999;

docs.title: derp.server.region_code
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_REGION_CODE

The region's short code, shown by Tailscale clients.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
derp:
  server:
    region_code: headscale

services.headscale.settings.derp.server.region_code = "headscale";

  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_REGION_NAME

The region's name, shown by Tailscale clients.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
derp:
  server:

export HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_REGION_NAME='Headscale Embedded DERP'

services.headscale.settings.derp.server.region_name = "Headscale Embedded DERP";

docs.title: derp.server.verify_clients
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: true
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_VERIFY_CLIENTS

Admits only nodes registered with this server.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
derp:
  server:

services.headscale.settings.derp.server.verify_clients = false;

docs.title: derp.server.stun_listen_addr
docs.text:
• Type: listen address
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_STUN_LISTEN_ADDR

The UDP host:port of the STUN server, which helps clients with NAT traversal; required when derp.server.enabled is true.

docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH

The file holding the DERP server's private key, relative to the configuration file; required when derp.server.enabled is true. A missing file is created with a new key. It must differ from noise.private_key_path.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS

services.headscale.settings.derp.server.private_key_path = "/var/lib/headscale/derp_server_private.key";

docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_IPV4

The server's public IPv4 address, published in the DERP map so clients reach it without DNS. Empty publishes none.

The server's public IPv6 address, published in the DERP map so clients reach it without DNS. Empty publishes none.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS

services.headscale.settings.derp.server.ipv6 = "2001:db8::1";

docs.title: derp.server.automatically_add_embedded_derp_region
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: true
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DERP_SERVER_AUTOMATICALLY_ADD_EMBEDDED_DERP_REGION

Adds the embedded server's region to the DERP map. When it is false and derp.server.enabled is true, derp.paths is required: write the region there yourself.

docs.text:
• Type: enum: sqlite, sqlite3, postgres

Logs a query that finds no record as an ordinary query, not as an error.

An empty host, name, user, pass or ssl leaves that setting to the driver, which reads the PG* environment variables and falls back to the defaults of libpq, PostgreSQL's client library: a local socket, the OS user, and TLS if the server offers it.

All database.postgres keys and defaults 
database:

    host: ""
    port: 0
    name: ""
    user: ""

docs.title: dns
docs.text:
The DNS configuration sent to clients, MagicDNS included, and TLS certificates for nodes. Clients apply it only with --accept-dns, their default. See DNS.

Replaces dns_config (removed).

All dns keys and defaults 
dns:
  magic_dns: true
  base_domain: tailnet.internal
  override_local_dns: true
  nameservers:
    global: []
    split: {}
  search_domains: []
  extra_records: []
  extra_records_path: ""
  certificates:
    enabled: false
    zone: ""
  challenge:
    propagation_timeout: 2m
    resolvers:
      - 9.9.9.9:53
      - 149.112.112.112:53
    provider: {}

docs.title: dns.magic_dns
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: true
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_MAGIC_DNS

Gives each node a name below dns.base_domain, e.g. laptop.example.com, resolved by the client. It requires dns.base_domain.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  magic_dns: false

export HEADSCALE_DNS_MAGIC_DNS=false

services.headscale.settings.dns.magic_dns = false;

Replaces dns_config.magic_dns (removed).

docs.title: dns.base_domain
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: tailnet.internal
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_BASE_DOMAIN

The domain MagicDNS names live under, without a trailing dot, e.g. example.com. The host of server_url must not be this domain or a name below it: clients take the domain over. The default is a private-use name, so dns.certificates needs a public domain you control.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  base_domain: tailnet.example.com

export HEADSCALE_DNS_BASE_DOMAIN=tailnet.example.com

services.headscale.settings.dns.base_domain = "tailnet.example.com";

Replaces dns_config.base_domain (removed).

docs.title: dns.override_local_dns
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: true
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_OVERRIDE_LOCAL_DNS

Makes clients use dns.nameservers.global instead of their local DNS settings; with no global nameserver there is nothing to override with, and clients keep their own. False sends them only as fallback resolvers.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  override_local_dns: false

export HEADSCALE_DNS_OVERRIDE_LOCAL_DNS=false

services.headscale.settings.dns.override_local_dns = false;

Replaces dns_config.override_local_dns (removed).

docs.title: dns.nameservers
docs.text:
The upstream DNS servers sent to clients. An entry that is neither an IP address nor a URL is skipped with a warning.

All dns.nameservers keys and defaults 
dns:
  nameservers:
    global: []
    split: {}

docs.title: dns.nameservers.global
docs.text:
• Type: list of strings
  • Default: []
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_NAMESERVERS_GLOBAL (space-separated or JSON array)

The nameservers for names dns.nameservers.split does not cover: IP addresses, or DNS-over-HTTPS URLs such as https://dns.nextdns.io/<id>. Empty by default, so clients keep their own DNS: headscale points them at no resolver you did not list.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  nameservers:
    global:
      - 9.9.9.9
      - 149.112.112.112
      - 2620:fe::fe
      - 2620:fe::9

export HEADSCALE_DNS_NAMESERVERS_GLOBAL='["9.9.9.9","149.112.112.112","2620:fe::fe","2620:fe::9"]'

services.headscale.settings.dns.nameservers.global = [
  "9.9.9.9"
  "149.112.112.112"
  "2620:fe::fe"
  "2620:fe::9"
];

Replaces dns_config.nameservers (removed).

docs.title: dns.nameservers.split
docs.text:
• Type: map of <domain> → list of strings
  • Default: {}
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_NAMESERVERS_SPLIT (JSON object)

Maps a domain to the nameservers that answer for it (split DNS). Domains are lowercased on load; two that differ only in case are an error.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  nameservers:
    split:
      corp.example.com:
        - 192.0.2.53
      lab.example.net:
        - 198.51.100.53
        - 2001:db8::53

export HEADSCALE_DNS_NAMESERVERS_SPLIT='{"corp.example.com":["192.0.2.53"],"lab.example.net":["198.51.100.53","2001:db8::53"]}'

services.headscale.settings.dns.nameservers.split = {
  "corp.example.com" = [
    "192.0.2.53"
  ];
  "lab.example.net" = [
    "198.51.100.53"
    "2001:db8::53"
  ];
};

Replaces dns_config.restricted_nameservers (removed). Replaces dns.split (removed).

docs.title: dns.search_domains
docs.text:
• Type: list of strings
  • Default: []
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_SEARCH_DOMAINS (space-separated or JSON array)

DNS search domains sent to clients. With MagicDNS, dns.base_domain comes first.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  search_domains:
    - corp.example.com
    - lab.example.net

export HEADSCALE_DNS_SEARCH_DOMAINS='["corp.example.com","lab.example.net"]'

services.headscale.settings.dns.search_domains = [
  "corp.example.com"
  "lab.example.net"
];

Replaces dns_config.domains (removed).

docs.title: dns.extra_records
docs.text:
• Type: list of DNS records
  • Default: []
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_EXTRA_RECORDS (JSON array)

DNS records served to clients, each with a name, type and value. Clients support A and AAAA. Mutually exclusive with dns.extra_records_path. See Setting extra DNS records.

Field Type Description name string The fully qualified domain name, e.g. grafana.example.com; the trailing dot is optional. type string The record type, A or AAAA; empty picks it from value. Clients ignore other types. value string The IP address the name resolves to. YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  extra_records:
    - name: grafana.tailnet.example.com
      type: A
      value: 100.64.0.3
    - name: grafana.tailnet.example.com
      type: AAAA
      value: fd7a:115c:a1e0::3

export HEADSCALE_DNS_EXTRA_RECORDS='[{"name":"grafana.tailnet.example.com","type":"A","value":"100.64.0.3"},{"name":"grafana.tailnet.example.com","type":"AAAA","value":"fd7a:115c:a1e0::3"}]'

services.headscale.settings.dns.extra_records = [
  {
    name = "grafana.tailnet.example.com";
    type = "A";
    value = "100.64.0.3";
  }
  {
    name = "grafana.tailnet.example.com";
    type = "AAAA";
    value = "fd7a:115c:a1e0::3";
  }
];

Replaces dns_config.extra_records (removed).

docs.title: dns.extra_records_path
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_EXTRA_RECORDS_PATH

A file of extra records, reloaded when it changes. The extension picks the format: .json, .hujson, .yaml or .yml. Mutually exclusive with dns.extra_records.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  extra_records_path: /var/lib/headscale/extra-records.json

export HEADSCALE_DNS_EXTRA_RECORDS_PATH=/var/lib/headscale/extra-records.json

services.headscale.settings.dns.extra_records_path = "/var/lib/headscale/extra-records.json";

docs.title: dns.certificates
docs.text:
Lets nodes get TLS certificates for their MagicDNS names with tailscale cert. The node runs ACME itself; headscale publishes its DNS-01 challenge through dns.challenge.provider.

All dns.certificates keys and defaults 
dns:
  certificates:
    enabled: false
    zone: ""

docs.title: dns.certificates.enabled
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: false
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_CERTIFICATES_ENABLED

Lets nodes run tailscale cert. It requires dns.magic_dns, a lowercase dns.base_domain and dns.challenge.provider.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  certificates:
    enabled: true

export HEADSCALE_DNS_CERTIFICATES_ENABLED=true

services.headscale.settings.dns.certificates.enabled = true;

docs.title: dns.certificates.zone
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_CERTIFICATES_ZONE

The public DNS zone challenge records are written to, when dns.base_domain sits below the zone apex. It must contain dns.base_domain. Empty uses dns.base_domain.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  certificates:
    zone: example.com

export HEADSCALE_DNS_CERTIFICATES_ZONE=example.com

services.headscale.settings.dns.certificates.zone = "example.com";

docs.title: dns.challenge
docs.text:
The DNS provider answering ACME DNS-01 challenges, for node certificates and for headscale's own certificate when tls.acme.challenge_type is DNS-01. See DNS-01 challenge provider.

All dns.challenge keys and defaults 
dns:
  challenge:
    propagation_timeout: 2m
    resolvers:
      - 9.9.9.9:53
      - 149.112.112.112:53
    provider: {}

docs.title: dns.challenge.propagation_timeout
docs.text:
• Type: duration
  • Default: 2m
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_PROPAGATION_TIMEOUT

How long to wait for a challenge record to show up on every authoritative nameserver. Zero skips the check.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  challenge:
    propagation_timeout: 5m

export HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_PROPAGATION_TIMEOUT=5m

services.headscale.settings.dns.challenge.propagation_timeout = "5m";

docs.title: dns.challenge.resolvers
docs.text:
• Type: list of strings
  • Default: ['9.9.9.9:53', '149.112.112.112:53']
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_RESOLVERS (space-separated or JSON array)

The servers asked for the zone's nameservers, each an IP or host with an optional port (53 if omitted). Empty uses the default public resolvers. The system resolver is never used: on a host running MagicDNS it answers for dns.base_domain itself.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  challenge:
    resolvers:
      - 9.9.9.9:53
      - '[2620:fe::fe]:53'

export HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_RESOLVERS='["9.9.9.9:53","[2620:fe::fe]:53"]'

services.headscale.settings.dns.challenge.resolvers = [
  "9.9.9.9:53"
  "[2620:fe::fe]:53"
];

docs.title: dns.challenge.provider
docs.text:
• Type: map of <setting> → value
  • Default: {}
  • Env: HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_PROVIDER (JSON object)

The DNS provider that writes challenge records: name selects it, the other keys are its settings. Keys are lowercased on load, at every depth; two that differ only in case are an error. Any setting may be file:<path> to read it from a file; a non-string one, such as acme-dns config, is the JSON in it. headscale generate config --running and /debug/config show name and file: references; every other setting is <redacted>, as any may be a credential. See DNS-01 challenge provider to set a provider up, acme-dns included, and to set it from environment variables.

Provider Settings acmedns config, password, server_url, subdomain, username cloudflare api_token, zone_token gigahost api_key hetzner api_token powerdns api_token, debug, server_id, server_url rfc2136 key, key_alg, key_name, server

Each text setting can also be set on its own as HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_PROVIDER_<SETTING>, e.g. HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_PROVIDER_API_TOKEN, which wins over the same setting in HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_PROVIDER and in the configuration file. An object setting, such as the config of acmedns, goes inside the JSON object of HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_PROVIDER; see Environment variables.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
dns:
  challenge:
    provider:
      api_token: file:/run/secrets/cloudflare
      name: cloudflare

export HEADSCALE_DNS_CHALLENGE_PROVIDER='{"api_token":"file:/run/secrets/cloudflare","name":"cloudflare"}'

services.headscale.settings.dns.challenge.provider = {
  api_token = "file:\${CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY}/dns_challenge_provider_api_token";
  name = "cloudflare";
};
systemd.services.headscale.serviceConfig.LoadCredential = [ "dns_challenge_provider_api_token:/run/secrets/cloudflare" ];

docs.title: tls
docs.text:
Headscale's own HTTPS certificate on listen_addr: from the files tls.cert_path and tls.key_path, or from ACME in tls.acme, not both. Without either, the server speaks plain HTTP. See TLS.

All tls keys and defaults 
tls:
  cert_path: ""
  key_path: ""
  acme:
    hostname: ""
    challenge_type: HTTP-01
    http_listen: :http
    url: ""
    email: ""
    cache_dir: /var/lib/headscale/cache

docs.title: tls.cert_path
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TLS_CERT_PATH

The PEM certificate file, relative to the configuration file. Setting it turns TLS on.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tls:
  cert_path: /etc/headscale/tls/cert.pem

export HEADSCALE_TLS_CERT_PATH=/etc/headscale/tls/cert.pem

services.headscale.settings.tls.cert_path = "/etc/headscale/tls/cert.pem";

Replaces tls_cert_path (removed).

docs.title: tls.key_path
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TLS_KEY_PATH

The PEM private key file of tls.cert_path, relative to the configuration file.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tls:
  key_path: /etc/headscale/tls/key.pem

export HEADSCALE_TLS_KEY_PATH=/etc/headscale/tls/key.pem

services.headscale.settings.tls.key_path = "/etc/headscale/tls/key.pem";

Replaces tls_key_path (removed).

docs.title: tls.acme
docs.text:
Gets the certificate from an ACME CA such as Let's Encrypt, and renews it. Setting tls.acme.hostname turns it on.

All tls.acme keys and defaults 
tls:
  acme:
    hostname: ""
    challenge_type: HTTP-01
    http_listen: :http
    url: ""
    email: ""
    cache_dir: /var/lib/headscale/cache

docs.title: tls.acme.hostname
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_HOSTNAME

The domain to request a certificate for. Setting it turns ACME on.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tls:
  acme:
    hostname: headscale.example.com

export HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_HOSTNAME=headscale.example.com

services.headscale.settings.tls.acme.hostname = "headscale.example.com";

Replaces tls_letsencrypt_hostname (removed).

docs.title: tls.acme.challenge_type
docs.text:
• Type: enum: HTTP-01, TLS-ALPN-01, DNS-01
  • Default: HTTP-01
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_CHALLENGE_TYPE

How the CA verifies that headscale controls tls.acme.hostname.

Value Meaning HTTP-01 Has the CA fetch a token over HTTP on port 80, answered on tls.acme.http_listen. TLS-ALPN-01 on listen_addr stays enabled too. TLS-ALPN-01 Has the CA check a special certificate on port 443, answered on listen_addr, which must be reachable there. DNS-01 Has the CA look up a TXT record, which headscale writes through dns.challenge.provider. It needs no open port. YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tls:
  acme:
    challenge_type: TLS-ALPN-01

export HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_CHALLENGE_TYPE=TLS-ALPN-01

services.headscale.settings.tls.acme.challenge_type = "TLS-ALPN-01";

Replaces tls_letsencrypt_challenge_type (removed).

docs.title: tls.acme.http_listen
docs.text:
• Type: listen address
  • Default: :http
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_HTTP_LISTEN

The host:port serving HTTP-01 challenges; the port may be a name, as in :http for port 80. Other requests to it are redirected to server_url.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tls:
  acme:
    http_listen: 0.0.0.0:80

export HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_HTTP_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:80

services.headscale.settings.tls.acme.http_listen = "0.0.0.0:80";

Replaces tls_letsencrypt_listen (removed).

docs.title: tls.acme.url
docs.text:
• Type: URL
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_URL

The CA's ACME directory. Empty uses Let's Encrypt.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tls:
  acme:
    url: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory

export HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_URL=https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory

services.headscale.settings.tls.acme.url = "https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory";

Replaces acme_url (removed).

docs.title: tls.acme.email
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_EMAIL

The contact address registered with the CA.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tls:
  acme:
    email: admin@example.com

export HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_EMAIL=admin@example.com

services.headscale.settings.tls.acme.email = "admin@example.com";

Replaces acme_email (removed).

docs.title: tls.acme.cache_dir
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: /var/lib/headscale/cache
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_CACHE_DIR

Where certificates and ACME account data are stored, relative to the configuration file.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tls:
  acme:
    cache_dir: /var/cache/headscale/acme

export HEADSCALE_TLS_ACME_CACHE_DIR=/var/cache/headscale/acme

services.headscale.settings.tls.acme.cache_dir = "/var/cache/headscale/acme";

Replaces tls_letsencrypt_cache_dir (removed).

docs.title: oidc
docs.text:
Login through an OpenID Connect provider. Setting oidc.issuer turns it on and requires oidc.client_id and oidc.client_secret. See OpenID Connect.

All oidc keys and defaults 
oidc:
  only_start_if_oidc_is_available: true
  issuer: ""
  client_id: ""
  client_secret: ""
  scope:
    - openid
    - profile
    - email
  extra_params: {}
  allowed_domains: []
  allowed_users: []
  allowed_groups: []
  email_verified_required: true
  use_expiry_from_token: false
  pkce:
    enabled: false
    method: S256

docs.title: oidc.only_start_if_oidc_is_available
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: true
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_ONLY_START_IF_OIDC_IS_AVAILABLE

Stops startup when the provider cannot be reached. False starts without OIDC, with CLI-based registration.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  only_start_if_oidc_is_available: false

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_ONLY_START_IF_OIDC_IS_AVAILABLE=false

services.headscale.settings.oidc.only_start_if_oidc_is_available = false;

docs.title: oidc.issuer
docs.text:
• Type: URL
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_ISSUER

The provider's issuer URL. Setting it turns OIDC on.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  issuer: https://idp.example.com/realms/headscale

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_ISSUER=https://idp.example.com/realms/headscale

services.headscale.settings.oidc.issuer = "https://idp.example.com/realms/headscale";

docs.title: oidc.client_id
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_CLIENT_ID

The client ID from the provider; required when oidc.issuer is set.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  client_id: headscale

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=headscale

services.headscale.settings.oidc.client_id = "headscale";

docs.title: oidc.client_secret
docs.text:
• Type: secret
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET

The client secret from the provider, or file:<path> to read it from a file; required when oidc.issuer is set. headscale generate config --running and /debug/config show a literal secret as <redacted> and a file: reference as written.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  client_secret: file:/run/secrets/oidc_client_secret

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=file:/run/secrets/oidc_client_secret

services.headscale.settings.oidc.client_secret = "file:\${CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY}/oidc_client_secret";
systemd.services.headscale.serviceConfig.LoadCredential = [ "oidc_client_secret:/run/secrets/oidc_client_secret" ];

Replaces oidc.client_secret_path (removed).

docs.title: oidc.scope
docs.text:
• Type: list of strings
  • Default: [openid, profile, email]
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_SCOPE (space-separated or JSON array)

The scopes requested; include openid.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  scope:
    - openid
    - profile
    - email
    - groups

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_SCOPE='["openid","profile","email","groups"]'

services.headscale.settings.oidc.scope = [
  "openid"
  "profile"
  "email"
  "groups"
];

docs.title: oidc.extra_params
docs.text:
• Type: map of <param> → string
  • Default: {}
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_EXTRA_PARAMS (JSON object)

Sent as is to the provider's authorization endpoint, e.g. domain_hint; names keep their case.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  extra_params:
    domain_hint: example.com
    prompt: select_account

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_EXTRA_PARAMS='{"domain_hint":"example.com","prompt":"select_account"}'

services.headscale.settings.oidc.extra_params = {
  domain_hint = "example.com";
  prompt = "select_account";
};

docs.title: oidc.allowed_domains
docs.text:
• Type: list of strings
  • Default: []
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS (space-separated or JSON array)

Admits only users whose email domain is listed. Empty admits any domain.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  allowed_domains:
    - example.com

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS='["example.com"]'

services.headscale.settings.oidc.allowed_domains = [
  "example.com"
];

docs.title: oidc.allowed_users
docs.text:
• Type: list of strings
  • Default: []
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_ALLOWED_USERS (space-separated or JSON array)

Admits only users whose email address is listed. Empty admits any user.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  allowed_users:
    - alice@example.com

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_ALLOWED_USERS='["alice@example.com"]'

services.headscale.settings.oidc.allowed_users = [
  "alice@example.com"
];

docs.title: oidc.allowed_groups
docs.text:
• Type: list of strings
  • Default: []
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_ALLOWED_GROUPS (space-separated or JSON array)

Admits only members of at least one listed group, from the provider's groups claim: UserInfo first, the ID token as fallback. Empty admits any group.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  allowed_groups:
    - headscale-users

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_ALLOWED_GROUPS='["headscale-users"]'

services.headscale.settings.oidc.allowed_groups = [
  "headscale-users"
];

docs.title: oidc.email_verified_required
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: true
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_EMAIL_VERIFIED_REQUIRED

Trusts an email only when the provider marks it verified: an unverified one fails oidc.allowed_domains and oidc.allowed_users and is not copied to the user. Turn it off for a provider that does not send email_verified.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  email_verified_required: false

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_EMAIL_VERIFIED_REQUIRED=false

services.headscale.settings.oidc.email_verified_required = false;

docs.title: oidc.use_expiry_from_token
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: false
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_USE_EXPIRY_FROM_TOKEN

Expires an OIDC-registered node with its token, instead of node.expiry. Tokens are often short-lived, forcing frequent logins.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  use_expiry_from_token: true

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_USE_EXPIRY_FROM_TOKEN=true

services.headscale.settings.oidc.use_expiry_from_token = true;

docs.title: oidc.pkce
docs.text:
Proof Key for Code Exchange (RFC 7636), which protects the authorization code from interception. See Enable PKCE.

All oidc.pkce keys and defaults 
oidc:
  pkce:
    enabled: false
    method: S256

docs.title: oidc.pkce.enabled
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: false
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_PKCE_ENABLED

Sends a PKCE challenge with each login.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  pkce:
    enabled: true

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_PKCE_ENABLED=true

services.headscale.settings.oidc.pkce.enabled = true;

docs.title: oidc.pkce.method
docs.text:
• Type: enum: plain, S256
  • Default: S256
  • Env: HEADSCALE_OIDC_PKCE_METHOD

How the code challenge is derived from the verifier. The verifier is sent as is in the token exchange.

Value Meaning plain Sends the verifier itself as the challenge. Use it only with a provider that does not support S256. S256 Sends the base64url SHA-256 of the verifier as the challenge. Recommended. YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
oidc:
  pkce:
    method: plain

export HEADSCALE_OIDC_PKCE_METHOD=plain

services.headscale.settings.oidc.pkce.method = "plain";

docs.title: logtail
docs.text:
Whether nodes send their logs to Tailscale.

All logtail keys and defaults 
logtail:
  enabled: false

docs.title: logtail.enabled
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: false
  • Env: HEADSCALE_LOGTAIL_ENABLED

Lets nodes send their logs to Tailscale Inc.; headscale cannot point them at another log server. False tells nodes not to.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
logtail:
  enabled: true

export HEADSCALE_LOGTAIL_ENABLED=true

services.headscale.settings.logtail.enabled = true;

docs.title: taildrop
docs.text:
Taildrop, Tailscale's file sharing between nodes.

All taildrop keys and defaults 
taildrop:
  enabled: true

docs.title: taildrop.enabled
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: true
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TAILDROP_ENABLED

Gives every node the file-sharing capability. False omits it from the baseline; a policy nodeAttrs grant can still give it.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
taildrop:
  enabled: false

export HEADSCALE_TAILDROP_ENABLED=false

services.headscale.settings.taildrop.enabled = false;

docs.title: auto_update
docs.text:
The tailnet-wide default for client auto-updates.

All auto_update keys and defaults 
auto_update:
  enabled: false

docs.title: auto_update.enabled
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: false
  • Env: HEADSCALE_AUTO_UPDATE_ENABLED

Makes auto-update the default for clients that have not chosen locally. Clients store the default they first see, so a later change reaches only new clients.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
auto_update:
  enabled: true

export HEADSCALE_AUTO_UPDATE_ENABLED=true

services.headscale.settings.auto_update.enabled = true;

docs.title: cli
docs.text:
How the headscale CLI reaches the server: the local unix_socket without authentication, or a remote cli.address with cli.api_key. The CLI reads these keys from its own configuration, such as ~/.config/headscale/config.yaml, or from HEADSCALE_CLI_* variables; the server does not read them, so on NixOS they do not belong in services.headscale.settings. See Remote control.

All cli keys and defaults 
cli:
  address: ""
  api_key: ""
  timeout: 5s
  insecure: false

docs.title: cli.address
docs.text:
• Type: string
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_CLI_ADDRESS

The remote server's host:port or URL; https:// is assumed without a scheme. Empty uses unix_socket.

YAMLEnvironment 
cli:
  address: headscale.example.com:443

export HEADSCALE_CLI_ADDRESS=headscale.example.com:443

docs.title: cli.api_key
docs.text:
• Type: secret
  • Default: ""
  • Env: HEADSCALE_CLI_API_KEY

The API key the CLI sends to cli.address, or file:<path> to read it from a file. Read only by the CLI.

YAMLEnvironment 
cli:
  api_key: file:/run/secrets/headscale_api_key

export HEADSCALE_CLI_API_KEY=file:/run/secrets/headscale_api_key

docs.title: cli.timeout
docs.text:
• Type: duration
  • Default: 5s
  • Env: HEADSCALE_CLI_TIMEOUT

Bounds each CLI command's requests to the server.

YAMLEnvironment 
cli:
  timeout: 30s

export HEADSCALE_CLI_TIMEOUT=30s

docs.title: cli.insecure
docs.text:
• Type: boolean
  • Default: false
  • Env: HEADSCALE_CLI_INSECURE

Skips TLS certificate verification of cli.address.

YAMLEnvironment 
cli:
  insecure: true

export HEADSCALE_CLI_INSECURE=true

docs.title: tuning
docs.text:
Holds performance settings that rarely need changing.

All tuning keys and defaults 
tuning:
  batch_change_delay: 800ms
  node_mapsession_buffered_chan_size: 30
  batcher_workers: 0
  register_cache_expiration: 15m
  register_cache_max_entries: 1024
  node_store_batch_size: 100
  node_store_batch_timeout: 500ms

docs.title: tuning.batch_change_delay
docs.text:
• Type: duration
  • Default: 800ms
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TUNING_BATCH_CHANGE_DELAY

How often queued changes are sent to clients as one update; must be positive.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tuning:
  batch_change_delay: 500ms

export HEADSCALE_TUNING_BATCH_CHANGE_DELAY=500ms

services.headscale.settings.tuning.batch_change_delay = "500ms";

docs.title: tuning.node_mapsession_buffered_chan_size
docs.text:
• Type: integer
  • Default: 30
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TUNING_NODE_MAPSESSION_BUFFERED_CHAN_SIZE

How many map updates are queued per connected client.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tuning:
  node_mapsession_buffered_chan_size: 60

export HEADSCALE_TUNING_NODE_MAPSESSION_BUFFERED_CHAN_SIZE=60

services.headscale.settings.tuning.node_mapsession_buffered_chan_size = 60;

docs.title: tuning.batcher_workers
docs.text:
• Type: integer
  • Default: 0 (three quarters of the CPU cores, at least one)
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TUNING_BATCHER_WORKERS

The number of workers building map updates for connected clients. Zero picks the number from the CPU count.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tuning:
  batcher_workers: 8

export HEADSCALE_TUNING_BATCHER_WORKERS=8

services.headscale.settings.tuning.batcher_workers = 8;

docs.title: tuning.register_cache_expiration
docs.text:
• Type: duration
  • Default: 15m
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TUNING_REGISTER_CACHE_EXPIRATION

How long a pending registration waits to be completed. Zero uses the default.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tuning:
  register_cache_expiration: 30m

export HEADSCALE_TUNING_REGISTER_CACHE_EXPIRATION=30m

services.headscale.settings.tuning.register_cache_expiration = "30m";

docs.title: tuning.register_cache_max_entries
docs.text:
• Type: integer
  • Default: 1024
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TUNING_REGISTER_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES

Bounds pending registrations. At capacity, new registrations are refused without evicting pending ones; SSH checks have a small reserve beyond it. Zero uses the default. See Pending authentication limits.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tuning:
  register_cache_max_entries: 4096

export HEADSCALE_TUNING_REGISTER_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES=4096

services.headscale.settings.tuning.register_cache_max_entries = 4096;

docs.title: tuning.node_store_batch_size
docs.text:
• Type: integer
  • Default: 100
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TUNING_NODE_STORE_BATCH_SIZE

How many node changes are batched before the in-memory node state, peer relationships included, is rebuilt; must be positive. Higher values save CPU on bulk changes but delay each change until its batch is full or tuning.node_store_batch_timeout passes.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tuning:
  node_store_batch_size: 200

export HEADSCALE_TUNING_NODE_STORE_BATCH_SIZE=200

services.headscale.settings.tuning.node_store_batch_size = 200;

docs.title: tuning.node_store_batch_timeout
docs.text:
• Type: duration
  • Default: 500ms
  • Env: HEADSCALE_TUNING_NODE_STORE_BATCH_TIMEOUT

The longest a partial batch of node changes waits before the rebuild; must be positive. Lower values answer single changes faster at the cost of more rebuilds.

YAMLEnvironmentNixOS 
tuning:
  node_store_batch_timeout: 1s

export HEADSCALE_TUNING_NODE_STORE_BATCH_TIMEOUT=1s

services.headscale.settings.tuning.node_store_batch_timeout = "1s";

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• Headscale loads its configuration from a YAML file

  • Validate the configuration file with: headscale configtest
